title: Attack search
text: Attacker Attack search An attack is a chain of at most k edits. The search space is a tree, harm over it is not submodular, and Aegis searches it with a bandit at every node. On this page Operators and units Feasible chains What the attacker knows Why greedy is not enough UCT: a bandit at every node Operators and units Primitive Effect remove_concept(c) Remove a class and every triple touching it remove_relation(s, p, o) Remove one triple inject_concept(c) Add a class inject_relation(s, p, o) Add a triple between existing classes Attackers use primitives in units: a removal ; a rewire (remove A ⊑ B , inject A ⊑ B' ); a flood (inject look-alikes such as Metall and attach them). candidate_units builds removal and rewire units over the elements with the largest impact, and flood units with flood=n ; rewires that would close a cycle are left out. Feasible chains A chain is feasible under budget k when each action applies in the state the earlier ones left, its cost is at most k , it changes at least one triple, and its harm is positive. Problem 1 is to find the feasible chain of largest harm. The cheapest chain whose harm reaches a threshold gives a workload's robustness radius : the fewest edits that make the agent answer wrongly. What the attacker knows Attacker Knows An evaluation of harm is White box Ontology, workload, gold answers Exact and cheap Gray box Ontology, workload, an impact ranking Exact, guided by the ranking Black box Only the agent's answers A costly, noisy agent call In every case the scarce resource is harm evaluations, so Aegis compares searches at equal evaluation counts. Every search returns a ScoredChain with its harm and evaluations ; states are cached by digest, so two orders that reach the same state cost one evaluation. Why greedy is not enough The look-alike Metall does no harm alone, and the triple that attaches it cannot be added before it exists. Together they put a wrong class into an answer. Harm is therefore not submodular, greedy selection has no approximation guarantee, and greedy stops as soon as no single next unit raises harm. UCT: a bandit at every node The root of the tree is the honest ontology; a node's children are the units that apply and fit the budget. uct treats the choice of the next unit as a multi-armed bandit and repeats four steps until its evaluation budget is spent: Select. Descend by UCB1: the child maximizing mean reward + c·√(ln N / n) , skipping exhausted subtrees. Expand. Open the next untried unit in impact order. Progressive widening allows at most ⌈N^0.5⌉ children for a node visited N times, so the search goes deep along the best-ranked units before it widens. Roll out. Finish the chain with random units and score it. Back up. Add the largest harm on the path (the attacker may stop at any prefix) to every node on it. UCT is anytime (it returns the best chain so far) and complete (with enough evaluations it expands every chain and returns the optimum). from aegis import beam, candidate_units, greedy, harm_over, random_chains, uct harm = harm_over(scorer_for, questions) units = candidate_units(onto, concept_deltas, relation_deltas, top=8) best = beam(harm, onto, units, budget=3, width=3, k=1)[0] found = uct(harm, onto, units, budget=3, evaluations=best.evaluations) # same cost as beam print(found.harm, [str(a) for a in found.chain]) Search Use greedy Baseline: the unit that raises harm most, until none does beam(width, k) The k most harmful distinct chains, keeping width partial chains per step random_chains(evaluations, seed) The floor: random chains until the budget is spent uct(evaluations, c, widening, seed) Bandit tree search; defaults c = 0.5 , widening = 0.5 Planned. Against a black-box agent, harm is a sampled estimate. The search will end with best-arm identification among its top chains, which returns a chain within ε of the most harmful with probability 1 − δ. Previous Concepts Next Protection

title: Concepts
text: Model Concepts The ontology is the matching semantics of a query over a fixed graph, so editing it changes answers without touching a fact. On this page Querying a graph with an ontology Quality and harm Affected area Impact Amplification Querying a graph with an ontology An ontology O = (C, R) has classes and triples, including subClassOf . A knowledge graph G has entities, edges, and asserted types. A query is a pattern whose nodes carry classes and whose edges carry properties. Under O , an entity matches a pattern node when one of its types falls under the node's class, and an edge matches when its property is the pattern's property or a subproperty of it. The answer Q_O(G) is the set of matches. The graph stays fixed; only the ontology changes. The same pattern on the same graph has different answers under different ontologies. Ontology-based entity matching (Ma et al., PVLDB 2019) relaxes class membership further, to ontological closeness above a threshold. Quality and harm A workload is a set of queries with gold answers. P_q(O) is the answer F1 of query q . The harm of moving from O to O' is the mean F1 drop over the workload: H(O, O') = mean over q of P_q(O) − P_q(O') It is measured over the workload, so an edit that breaks one answer while repairing another does not look harmless. In code: workload_harm and harm_over . Affected area After incremental graph pattern matching (Fan et al., SIGMOD 2011), the affected area of an ontology update is the set of matches it adds or removes: AFF_q = Q_O(G) △ Q_O'(G) . forensics.affected_area computes it per query, and forensics.attribute splits a chain's affected area across its actions. Locality. Inserting or deleting one triple A ⊑ B can change the classes under a pattern node only when that node's class is a superclass of B (or B itself), and then only by classes under A . The detector uses this to re-score only the queries an edit can reach. Impact The counterfactual impact of a class is Δ_c = P(O) − P(O \ c) , and Δ_r likewise for a triple: concept_impact , relation_impact . Group testing over subtrees ( group_impact ) gives the same values with fewer evaluations when few classes matter. An impact ranking is a defender's diagnostic and an attacker's map at once. Amplification Removing one asserted A ⊑ B can remove every inferred X ⊑ Y with X under A and Y above B . forensics.closure_delta reports the asserted and inferred triples a change touches and their ratio; on mouse anatomy, two removals change almost six inferred triples for each asserted one. title: Experiments
text: Results Experiments Each experiment is a script in experiments/ that writes a dated result file; the README and the white paper read from those files. On this page Experiments Attack search at equal cost Protection by locking A language-model agent Agent memory Experiments Script Measures Model calls real_ontologies/run.py Impact by group testing, the worst two-action chain, detection, inferred amplification None attack_defense/run.py Greedy, beam, random, and UCT at equal evaluations; residual harm under M locks None llm_agent/run.py A language-model agent answering the same workloads in words, honest and attacked 20 requests, $0.68 memory_defense/run.py Random attacks on a shared agent memory; repair by attribution against rollback None Every model call is recorded in results/costs/ledger.jsonl with tokens, seconds, and list-price dollars. Attack search at equal cost uv run python experiments/attack_defense/run.py --json results/attack_defense/2026-10-18.json uv run --with matplotlib python paper/figures.py results/attack_defense/2026-10-18.json At equal harm evaluations (beam's count), the most harmful three-action chain each search finds; random and UCT are means of 5 seeds. Ontology Greedy Beam Random UCT Evaluations EBSD 0.600 0.600 0.533 0.493 167 MatProc 0.619 1.000 0.776 0.805 119 XRD 0.444 0.444 0.533 0.600 91 Mouse anatomy 0.803 0.945 0.809 0.884 104 UCT beats greedy and beam on XRD at every budget from two actions up (0.763 against 0.644 at four), ties beam at two actions elsewhere, and trails it at three and four where harm is close to additive. Given 200 evaluations it reaches 1.000 on MatProc and 0.945 on mouse anatomy with no spread across seeds; random search still varies by 0.04 to 0.12. Protection by locking Residual harm of a two-action attacker (the best of beam and UCT) after locking six triples: Ontology No locks Random Top impact Best response EBSD 0.400 0.320 0.400 0.133 MatProc 0.800 0.459 0.025 0.025 XRD 0.400 0.400 0.212 0.030 Mouse anatomy 0.745 0.675 0.029 0.019 Best response is never worse than top impact. On EBSD, six top-impact locks change nothing because the attacker moves to the next query's triples. Ten well-chosen locks remove all of a two-action attacker's harm on every ontology. A language-model agent Claude Opus 5.5, writing SPARQL against a labeled schema, answers every honest question on all four ontologies and then suffers exactly the template answerer's harm under the worst two-action chain (0.400, 0.800, 0.400, and 0.745). On hierarchy questions the damage is in the ontology, so the cheap template answerer is a faithful proxy during attack search. Agent memory Over 20 random attacks of one to three forged or removed findings, every attack was detected. Repair by attribution restored every probe and kept all honest work done after the attack; rollback restored the probes and lost that work. Previous Recovery Next Leaderboard

title: Getting started
text: Setup Getting started Install Aegis, attack a small materials ontology, and roll the attack back. On this page Install A first attack From the command line From Python Install git clone https://github.com/lamng3/aegis.git cd aegis pip install -e ".[dev]" # Python 3.11 or newer, no runtime dependencies pip install -e ".[owl]" # optional: read OWL and Turtle with rdflib A first attack python examples/attack_and_recover.py most depended-on: [('Material', 1.0), ('Metal', 0.6)] workload harm: 0.602 remove_relation(('Metal', 'subClassOf', 'Material')): affected 3 result elements inject_relation(('Metal', 'subClassOf', 'Temperature')): affected 3 result elements inject_concept(Metall): affected 0 result elements inject_relation(('Metall', 'subClassOf', 'Material')): affected 1 result elements rolled back to lsn 2 | honest edit kept: True | healthy: True The example ranks the classes the workload depends on, runs a rewire and a flood, attributes the damage to each action, and rolls back to the last healthy state. The look-alike Metall does nothing until a relation attaches it: the same pair that defeats greedy search. From the command line aegis attack examples/materials.json examples/materials_workload.json --budget 2 aegis attack examples/materials.json examples/materials_workload.json --budget 2 --search uct Beam search finds a rewire of harm 0.600 on this example; UCT, at 200 harm evaluations, finds a chain of harm 1.000 that removes Material . Write the chains with --json chains.json and replay them under the detector: aegis detect examples/materials.json examples/materials_workload.json chains.json --threshold 0.05 From Python from aegis import ChainBuilder, HealthMonitor, Ontology, VersionedOntology, no_subclass_cycles onto = Ontology.of( ["Material", "Metal", "Alloy"], [("Metal", "subClassOf", "Material"), ("Alloy", "subClassOf", "Metal")], ) v = VersionedOntology(onto) monitor = HealthMonitor({"acyclic": no_subclass_cycles}) v.subscribe(monitor) # checks run on every commit v.apply_chain(ChainBuilder().add_concept("Steel").rewire("Alloy", "subClassOf", "Metal", "Material").build()) v.rollback_to(monitor.last_healthy()) # back to the newest healthy state Previous Overview Next Playground

title: Attack search, protection, and recovery for ontology-grounded agents
text: Attack search, protection, and recovery for ontology-grounded agents Aegis finds the ontology edits that hurt an agent most, chooses which triples to lock against them, and undoes the damage when an attack lands. $ git clone https://github.com/lamng3/aegis.git && cd aegis $ uv sync && uv run python examples/attack_and_recover.py Get started Playground Watch it work Experiments Attack, then defend recorded experiment results Try it: Drag the sliders: how many edits the attacker gets, and how many triples the defender locks. edits locks Harm runs from 0 to 1 over the ontology's query workload. Top bars: the most harmful chain each search finds. Bottom bars: harm left after the locks, against a two-edit attacker. The numbers come from results/attack_defense/2026-10-18.json ; this page computes nothing. Watch the attack search work A recorded run of the library's own search on a small ontology. The bandit grows its tree one iteration at a time while the ontology on the right is attacked. Pause, step, or switch to impact, greedy search, locking, or ontological matching. Open the full page . Loading the recorded run… What it does An agent reads its knowledge graph through an ontology. Aegis treats the ontology like data a database must defend. Showcase Watch the attack search work: the affected area, greedy, the bandit's tree, and the locks. Playground Attack a small ontology in the browser: edit it, search for the worst chain, find the damage, and roll back. Getting started Run the example: attack a small materials ontology, then recover. Concepts Counterfactual attacks, and the affected area that measures them. Attack search Greedy, beam, random, and UCT over the tree of edit chains. Protection Lock the triples that leave the attacker's best response least harmful. Recovery Find the last healthy state in the log and roll back, keeping honest edits. Experiments Four ontologies, with the numbers behind the demo. What it is An agent that answers questions over a knowledge graph reads the graph through an ontology. The ontology says which classes a query term covers and which links may be followed, so editing a few ontology triples changes the answers while every fact in the graph stays intact. Aegis studies that threat from both sides. Attack. Given a query workload and a budget of k edits, find the chain that lowers answer quality most. Aegis searches the tree of edit chains with greedy, beam, random, and UCT (a bandit at every node). Protection. Given room to lock M triples, choose the locks that leave the attacker's best response least harmful. Recovery. Every edit is a logged transaction with its undo. Aegis measures what each edit changed, detects the first harmful commit, and rolls back while keeping honest edits. Pages Getting started Install, attack a toy ontology, roll it back. Concepts Ontology-grounded queries, harm, and the affected area. Attack search Operators, feasible chains, and UCT. Protection Locking triples against a best response. Recovery Transactions, backends, detection, and repair. Experiments What each experiment measures and how to rerun it. Reference Commands, modules, and extension points. Install git clone https://github.com/lamng3/aegis.git cd aegis pip install -e ".[dev]" python examples/attack_and_recover.py The code is github.com/lamng3/aegis .

Defense: who leaves the least harm? How to read it Two boards, from the same experiment. In the first the strongest attacker ranks first: the search that finds the most harmful chain of edits at equal cost. In the second the best defense ranks first: the one that leaves the least harm. Aegis's own searches and defenses are highlighted next to the simple baselines they have to beat. Attack: who finds the worst chain? Defense: who leaves the least harm? How to read it Harm is the mean F1 drop over the five "What kinds of X are there?" queries, from 0 to 1. Attack compares the searches at equal evaluations: beam search runs to completion and sets the budget that random search and UCT get. Beam can win at small budgets; Attack search shows how UCT catches up as the budget grows. Defense is against a two-edit attacker. Residual harm is the best of beam search and UCT against the locked ontology, so a lock set is not credited for a chain the search missed. Click a column to sort. Ranks stay with the headline column. title: Playground
text: Try it Playground Attack a small ontology in your browser: edit it, let the library's search find the worst chain of edits, see which action did the damage, and roll back to the last healthy state. On this page Things to try What it keeps What runs where Everything runs in your browser. Aegis itself is Python and is not run here: the page runs a JavaScript port of the small materials example ( examples/attack_and_recover.py ): the ontology and its four edit primitives, the workload's F1 and harm, per-action attribution, the versioned log with rollback and last-healthy, and the library's greedy and beam attack searches. Its tests recompute the impacts, the candidate edits, the searches at four budgets, and 40 random edit chains against the Python and compare every number. The real ontologies, UCT search, protection by locking, and the memory defenses are not run here. Loading the playground… Things to try Press An honest edit , then The example attack . The workload's F1 falls, the harm is the mean drop, and Which action did what shows how many result elements each action changed. The first two actions rewire Metal under Temperature and affect the most result elements; the last two flood in a look-alike concept. Press Find the worst chain with beam search and a budget of two. The library's search proposes the most harmful chains it finds within the budget. Apply one and compare it with your own attack. In Recovery , the last healthy state is the one just before the attack, so rolling back keeps the honest edit. Roll back, then press Start over to compare with the original. What it keeps Your edits are saved in this browser (localStorage) and replayed when the page loads. Start over clears them. Nothing is sent anywhere. Previous Getting started Next Showcase

title: Protection
text: Defender Protection Lock M triples so that edits removing them go to a reviewer, and choose the locks that leave the attacker's best response least harmful. On this page What a lock does The problem Lock strategies The attacker oracle matters What a lock does A locked triple cannot be removed: remove_relation on it, and remove_concept on either of its ends, are queued for a human reviewer instead of being committed. Injections stay open, since a triple cannot be locked before it exists. Review capacity bounds the locks by M . from aegis import allowed open_units = allowed(units, locks) # the units an attacker can still run The problem The defender moves first and the attacker sees the locks: a leader–follower game. A lock set is judged by its residual harm , the harm of the attacker's best chain once the locks are in place, and the defender wants the lock set of at most M triples with the smallest residual. When harmful chains are listed explicitly, deciding whether M locks bring the residual below a threshold is Hitting Set. Lock strategies Function Locks lock_top_impact(deltas, m) The m triples with the largest Δ_r; cheap, blind to substitutes lock_random(deltas, m, seed) m triples drawn from those with Δ_r > 0; the floor lock_best_response(attacker, onto, units, m, deltas) One lock per round: run the attacker, then lock the triple of its best chain that leaves the smallest residual from aegis import beam, lock_best_response, residual, uct def attacker(us): found = beam(harm, onto, us, budget=2, width=3, k=1) found.append(uct(harm, onto, us, 2, 300)) return max(found, key=lambda s: s.harm) locks = lock_best_response(attacker, onto, units, 6, relation_deltas) print(residual(attacker, units, locks)) The attacker oracle matters Residual harm is only as good as the attacker that computes it. With beam search alone, locking triples on XRD steered beam to a chain more harmful than the one it found without locks, so locking appeared to raise the harm. Evaluate lock sets against the best of several searches, as above. Previous Attack search Next Recovery

title: Recovery
text: Substrate Recovery Aegis treats the ontology like a database treats its data: every edit is a logged transaction with its undo, checked on commit, and reversible. On this page Transactions and the log Storage backends Health checks and constraints Detection Decisions and repair Agent memory Transactions and the log VersionedOntology applies each action atomically with its undo actions; apply_chain is all or nothing. Every commit records digests of the state before and after, so any state can be rebuilt ( forensics.state_at ) and rollback checks it restored the exact prior state. v = VersionedOntology(onto) v.apply(inject_concept("Steel")) v.apply_chain([remove_relation("Alloy", "subClassOf", "Metal"), inject_relation("Alloy", "subClassOf", "Material")]) v.rollback_to(1) Storage backends Backend Stores Rollback MemoryBackend() Python lists Truncates the log JsonlBackend(dir) base.json and log.jsonl Truncates the log OntoDBBackend(dir, binary=...) Transactions on an RDF database, read back with SPARQL Compensating transactions in the database's write-ahead log migrate(src, dst) replays one backend's history into another. Health checks and constraints HealthMonitor runs checks on every commit: no_subclass_cycles , domain_range , disjoint , and an OWL reasoner's satisfiability ( aegis.reasoning.satisfiable ). VersionedOntology.constrain rejects an action before it reaches the log. Detection Detector re-scores only the queries a commit can reach, alarms when harm passes a threshold, rolls back to the commit before the first alarm, and keeps a Bloom filter of suspect classes. ScoreMonitor records the workload score per commit. Decisions and repair aegis.decide rejects a pending chain past a threshold, repairs committed damage by compensating the fewest commits that explain it while keeping later edits, and rolls back when repair cannot. Detector.accept makes a reviewed, honest state the new baseline. Agent memory aegis.memory applies the same attacks and defenses to a shared agent memory store: forged, removed, rewired, or tampered findings; impact per memory; guards on writers and provenance; and repair by attribution, which keeps honest work done after the attack. title: Showcase
text: Watch it work Showcase Replay a real run of the attack search on the small materials ontology, one step at a time: the impact of each element, greedy search, the bandit's search tree, the locks that defend, and what the attack does to ontological matching. What this is A recording of the library, not a simulation. experiments/walkthrough/trace.py runs Aegis's own impact ranking, greedy search, UCT, beam search, and best-response locking on the materials ontology of the playground , and writes every step down; this page replays it. Under the ontology, AFF is the affected area of the state shown, as forensics.affected_area computes it (after Fan et al., SIGMOD 2011): the answers each question lost and gained. Loading the recorded run… How to read it Impact. Two questions are asked of the ontology. Each element is taken out in turn and both are asked again: the drop in mean F1 is that element's Δ. The elements with Δ above zero glow. They are the vulnerable area, the part the answers depend on, and what an attacker picks first. The AFF line shows which answers each removal changes. Greedy. Add whichever unit raises harm most, until nothing does. It stops early, because each edit that matters here looks weak until the other has been made. Bandit. The tree grows downward from "no edits". Each card is a first edit, with its visits and mean harm. The card in play opens a second row: the second edits tried after it, each a card of its own; the others show how many were tried ("+3 next"). Red marks the path being walked, green the chain just opened, orange the rollout, and gold the best chain so far. Below the tree, the root's arms show the bandit's choice: each arm's UCB is its mean harm (solid) plus an exploration bonus that shrinks as the arm is visited (striped), and the highest UCB wins unless the root still has room to open a new arm. An arm whose every chain has been scored is marked explored and is no longer chosen. Lock. The defender has room for two locks. Each round takes the attacker's best chain, tries locking each triple it removes, and keeps the one that leaves the attacker the least harm. Ontological match. Ontological graph keys (Ma et al., "Ontology-based Entity Matching in Attributed Graphs", PVLDB 12(10), 2019) match a pattern node labelled l against every node whose label is within distance α of l in the ontology: the relevant set lsim( l ). The two worst chains are replayed against that matching. Rewiring Metal under MeltingPoint takes Metal and Alloy out of reach of Material and brings Metal within reach of Temperature, so graph nodes typed Metal stop matching one pattern and start matching another, though the graph was never touched. Aegis does not implement this matching; the trace writes out the paper's definition, with the weights of its Example 3 (0.3 for subClassOf, 0.6 for a descriptive relation) and α = 0.6. The best attack plan. Greedy, the bandit, and locking each end on the plan they leave you with, drawn as a path from the honest ontology through each edit: the harm so far, and the answers that edit changes. The numbers on the ontology mark where each edit lands; step through to watch them land one at a time. After locking, the plan is the attack the defender still faces. Keys: ← and → step, space plays. Drag the scrubber to jump to any step. Previous Playground Next Concepts
